t: Drywall taping and finishing in Toronto: Level 4 vs Level 5
d: The six drywall finish levels in plain words, when a Level 5 skim coat is worth paying for, and what should be in a finishing quote. Toronto and the GTA.
x: Service 03 · Level 4 & Level 5 Finishing Surfaces Ready for the Light. Finishing is where a wall becomes beautiful or ordinary. We tape, coat and sand to the level each room needs, with a full skim coat where light and paint demand it. Request an Estimate Builders — Send Your Drawings IN SHORT Ricarti Drywall finishes painted walls to Level 4 as standard and recommends Level 5, a full skim coat, where strong side light, tall walls, or dark or glossy paint would show the joints. We also remove popcorn ceilings, create smooth ceiling finishes and repair drywall and plaster. The finish level for each room is written into the estimate. Kent — smooth painted walls and ceiling. Level 4 or Level 5? Level 4 is three coats of joint compound over taped joints and fasteners, sanded smooth. It suits most painted rooms with flat or eggshell paint. Level 5 adds a thin skim coat over the entire surface. It evens out the difference between paper and compound, so joints do not show under raking light, on tall walls, or beneath dark or glossy paint. We recommend it only where it pays, and say so room by room. Technical capabilities What we deliver. Professional drywall taping Level 4 finishing Level 5 finishing Full-surface skim coating Smooth ceiling finishes Popcorn ceiling removal Drywall repairs and restoration Premium paint-ready surfaces Finishing for critical lighting conditions The finish levels The six finish levels, in plain words. The industry grades drywall finish from Level 0 to Level 5. Naming the level in the contract makes sure “paint-ready” means the same thing to you and to us. Level What is done Where it is used 0 Board hung. No tape or compound. Temporary walls 1 Tape set in compound at joints. Hidden areas, above ceilings 2 Tape plus one coat over joints and screws. Garages, under tile 3 A second coat over joints and screws. Under heavy texture 4 A third coat, sanded smooth. Most painted rooms: flat and eggshell paint 5 Level 4 plus a skim coat over the whole surface. Raking light, tall walls, curved walls, glossy or dark paint Materials and systems The right system for the job. Paper and mesh joint tape Chosen for each joint type, embedded in compound for a strong, crack-resistant seam. Joint compounds Setting-type and ready-mix compounds used where each performs best. Corner beads Paper-faced, metal or vinyl beads for straight, durable corners. Skim coat A thin coat over the entire surface for Level 5 finishes. Primer-ready surfaces Sanded, cleaned and checked under a work light before paint. Typical applications Where it makes the difference. Living rooms and great rooms with large windows Foyers and stair halls Ceilings under pot lights and skylights Rooms with dark or glossy paint Popcorn ceiling removal and smooth ceilings Repairs in older homes Kent — finish coats, floors protected. Lauther Ave — new ceiling around the original medallion. Thompson — skimming a ceiling. Benefits Why it matters. 01 A finish that disappears Walls and ceilings that read as flat, clean planes in any light. 02 Honest recommendations Level 5 only where light or paint will show the joints; Level 4 where it is enough. 03 Checked before paint Every surface inspected with a work light held flat to the wall. Questions Frequently asked. How much more does Level 5 cost than Level 4? + Level 5 adds a full coat of compound and the labour to sand it, so it costs more on the finishing line. Using it only where the light demands it keeps the cost down. Your estimate shows the finish level for each room. Can I tell the finish level by looking? + Hold a bright light flat against the wall, or look along it toward a window. Joints and screw heads that disappear face-on often show at that angle. It is how we check our own work. Can you remove popcorn ceilings? + Yes. Textured ceilings can be removed and refinished smooth, or covered with new drywall. Ceilings installed before the 1990s may contain asbestos. In Ontario, asbestos on construction projects is regulated under Ontario Regulation 278/05, which requires material that may contain asbestos to be identified before it is disturbed. We have the texture tested before any removal and plan the work around the result. Do you finish drywall hung by another company? + Yes, after we have looked at it. Poorly hung board costs more to finish well, and we will say so in the estimate. t: Lath and plaster in older Toronto homes: repair, cover or replace?
d: Patch, skim, overboard with drywall or strip to the studs: how to decide what to do with the plaster walls and ceilings in a pre-war Toronto house.
x: Lath and plaster in older Toronto homes: repair, cover or replace? Patch, skim, overboard with drywall or strip to the studs: how to decide what to do with the plaster walls and ceilings in a pre-war Toronto house. By Ricarti Drywall · 24 November 2026 Old plaster ceiling being removed to expose wood lath, Lauther Ave, Toronto. IN SHORT Small cracks and holes in sound plaster can be patched. Sagging or widely cracked ceilings are usually overboarded with drywall or stripped and replaced. Strip to the studs when the walls are open for wiring, plumbing or insulation anyway. Test for asbestos before disturbing old plaster or textured coatings. Much of Toronto's housing was built with plaster over wood lath: thin strips nailed across the studs, with plaster pushed through the gaps to grip. Done well, it lasts a century. When it starts to fail, homeowners face a choice between keeping it and replacing it, and the right answer depends on what is failing and what else is happening in the house. Repair: when the plaster is still sound Press gently on the wall or ceiling around a crack. If it feels solid, the plaster is still keyed to the lath and can be repaired: cracks taped and filled, holes patched with plaster or drywall inserts, and the area skimmed to blend. A former client wrote that we installed new drywall and also repaired a lath and plaster wall in the same house; the two can live side by side. Cover: overboarding If a ceiling sags or is cracked across its width, the plaster keys have probably broken. Rather than tearing it down, the ceiling can be screwed back to the joists and covered with a layer of drywall. This is less messy than demolition and keeps the old plaster as extra mass for sound. The trade-off is a small change in depth at trim, crown moulding and electrical boxes. Replace: strip to the studs Removing plaster makes sense when the walls must be opened anyway: new wiring, new plumbing, or insulating exterior walls that were never insulated. Once the studs are bare, insulation, a vapour barrier and new drywall bring the wall up to modern standards in one go. Open the wall only when it needs to be open. Then do everything inside it at once. Test before you disturb Some older plasters, joint compounds and textured ceiling coatings contain asbestos, and older paint layers may contain lead. Before any demolition or heavy sanding in an older home, have samples tested by a qualified lab. If they come back positive, removal must be handled under Ontario's asbestos regulations by people trained to do it. Keeping the character Plaster walls have a slightly softer, less perfect plane than new drywall, and that is part of an older home's character. When we patch or overboard next to original plaster, we feather the finish so the transition does not show. Crown mouldings and ceiling medallions can be protected and kept, as on a recent ceiling on Lauther Ave in Toronto. Not sure which route suits your house? t: Seven questions to ask a drywall contractor before you sign
d: Insurance, WSIB, finish level, who is on site, dust, schedule and payments: the questions that separate a good drywall quote from a cheap one.
x: Seven questions to ask a drywall contractor before you sign Insurance, WSIB, finish level, who is on site, dust, schedule and payments: the questions that separate a good drywall quote from a cheap one. By Ricarti Drywall · 24 November 2026 Kitchen and living area mid-renovation with finished drywall, Kent, Toronto. IN SHORT Ask for proof of liability insurance and a WSIB clearance certificate, the finish level for each room in writing, who will actually be on site, how dust and clean-up are handled, a schedule, and a payment plan tied to finished stages. Two drywall quotes for the same house can be thousands of dollars apart, and the cheaper one is not always cheaper by the time the paint goes on. These seven questions bring the difference into the open before you sign. 1. Can I see your insurance and WSIB clearance? A contractor working in your home should carry commercial liability insurance and be registered with the WSIB. Ask for the certificate of insurance and a current WSIB clearance certificate. If a worker is injured on your property and the contractor is not covered, the problem can become yours. 2. What finish level is included, room by room? Drywall finish is graded from Level 0 to Level 5. Most painted rooms are finished to Level 4; rooms with strong side light, tall walls or dark paint may need Level 5, a skim coat over the whole surface. A quote that does not name the level leaves the most visible part of the job undefined. Our finishing guide explains the levels. 3. Who will be on site, and who do I call? Ask whether the crew is the contractor's own or subcontracted, and who is the single person responsible for your job. You want one name and one phone number. 4. How do you handle dust and clean-up? Sanding drywall makes fine dust that travels. Ask how rooms are sealed off, whether floors are protected, and whether the site is swept and bagged daily or only at the end. 5. What is the schedule, and what happens if it slips? Ask for a start date, the time between board, tape and finish coats, and the date you can paint. Joint compound needs drying time between coats, so a schedule that looks too fast usually is. 6. What is not included? Common exclusions are corner bead upgrades, bulkheads, repairs to damaged framing, patching after other trades, primer and haul-away. None of these is wrong to exclude, but you should know before the job starts, not after. 7. How are payments staged? A fair plan ties payments to finished stages, such as board hung, taping complete and final walkthrough, with a modest deposit up front. Be cautious of anyone asking for most of the price before work begins. A good quote answers these questions before you ask them. Our written scopes cover all seven. t: Soundproofing a room: what actually works
d: Mass, decoupling, absorption and sealing: the four things that make a wall or ceiling quieter, and the popular fixes that do very little.
x: Soundproofing a room: what actually works Mass, decoupling, absorption and sealing: the four things that make a wall or ceiling quieter, and the popular fixes that do very little. By Ricarti Drywall · 24 November 2026 Mineral wool sound insulation behind steel resilient channel on a sloped ceiling, Stanton, Toronto. IN SHORT A quieter wall needs four things: more mass (extra or sound-rated board), decoupling (resilient channel or separate studs), absorption (mineral wool in the cavity) and airtight sealing with acoustic sealant. Foam panels and egg cartons change echo inside a room, not noise through the wall. Home offices, media rooms, nurseries next to a busy hallway, basement suites under a family room: more of our homeowner projects now include some kind of sound control. The good news is that the methods are well understood. The bad news is that a lot of what is sold as soundproofing does very little. The four things that work Mass Heavier walls move less when sound hits them. A second layer of drywall, or a sound-rated board, adds mass with very little loss of space. Decoupling If the drywall is screwed straight to the studs, vibration passes through the framing into the next room. Mounting the board on resilient channel or sound clips, or building a separate row of studs, breaks that path. Decoupling must be installed carefully: a single screw driven through the channel into a stud can undo most of the benefit. Absorption Mineral wool in the wall or ceiling cavity absorbs sound that would otherwise ring inside the hollow space. It is denser than fibreglass and does a better job. Sealing Sound travels through any gap air can pass through. Perimeter joints, electrical boxes and pipe penetrations are sealed with acoustic sealant, which stays flexible. Back-to-back outlets in a shared wall are a common weak spot. Mass, decoupling, absorption, sealing. Leave one out and the wall is only as good as its weakest part. What does not work Foam panels and egg cartons reduce echo inside a room. They do almost nothing to stop sound passing through a wall. Insulation alone in a standard wall helps a little, but without mass and decoupling the improvement is modest. Sealing nothing : a high-performance wall with an unsealed gap under the bottom plate leaks noise like an open door. Ceilings are the hard part Footsteps from the floor above are impact noise, carried through the joists. Mineral wool between the joists, resilient channel and two layers of board on the ceiling below make a real difference. Treating the floor above with an underlayment, where that is possible, helps more still. On a recent project on Stanton in Toronto we installed mineral wool and steel channel under a sloped ceiling before boarding. If you are planning a room that needs to be quiet, tell us at the site visit ; it is far cheaper to build in than to add later. Planning a project? We will walk it with you and put it in writing. t: Spray foam or batts: which goes where, and why
d: Closed-cell foam, open-cell foam, mineral wool and fibreglass batts compared for Toronto homes: where each one earns its cost, and where it does not.
x: Spray foam or batts: which goes where, and why Closed-cell foam, open-cell foam, mineral wool and fibreglass batts compared for Toronto homes: where each one earns its cost, and where it does not. By Ricarti Drywall · 24 November 2026 Closed-cell spray foam applied between roof rafters, Brule, Toronto. IN SHORT Use closed-cell spray foam where space is tight or moisture is a risk: rim joists, cathedral ceilings, below-grade walls. Batts, mineral wool or fibreglass, are the better value in ordinary stud walls and open attic floors. Most good houses use both. Most homeowners are told to choose between spray foam and batts as if it were one decision for the whole house. It is not. A well insulated house is usually a mix, and the skill is in putting each material where it works hardest for its cost. What each one does Material Roughly R per inch Air seal Best for Closed-cell spray foam R-6 to R-7 Yes Rim joists, cathedral ceilings, basement and below-grade walls, tight cavities Open-cell spray foam R-3.5 to R-4 Yes Interior sound control, unvented roof assemblies where the design allows it Mineral wool batts About R-4 No Exterior stud walls, sound walls and floors, near heat sources (it does not burn) Fibreglass batts R-3 to R-4 No Standard stud walls and open attic floors on a budget The numbers are typical ranges, not product ratings. The values your house must reach are set by your designer's energy compliance package under the Ontario Building Code, and your inspector checks against that. Where closed-cell foam earns its cost Closed-cell foam is expensive per square foot, but in a few places nothing else does the job as well. At the rim joist, where the floor framing meets the foundation, it seals the air leaks that make a basement cold and drafty. In a cathedral or sloped ceiling, where there is no attic to fill, it gives the most insulation in the least depth. On basement walls it stops warm indoor air from reaching the cold concrete, which is where condensation and mould begin. Foam where the house leaks or sweats. Batts where it simply needs to be warm. Where batts are the better buy In a standard 2×6 exterior wall, properly fitted batts with a continuous vapour barrier and sealed seams perform well for a fraction of the cost of foam. Fit is everything: a batt cut tight around every box and pipe, with no gaps or compression, does most of what the label promises. A batt stuffed in loosely does not. Mineral wool is our usual choice for walls between rooms and floors between storeys, because its density blocks sound far better than fibreglass. It also does not burn, which is why it is often used around chimneys and in fire-rated assemblies. The part people forget: the air barrier Batts slow heat, but air passes straight through them. In a cold climate the wall needs a continuous air and vapour barrier on the warm side, usually polyethylene with every seam and penetration taped or sealed. Inspectors check this before drywall goes up, and it is far cheaper to do it right then than to chase drafts later. What we usually recommend Closed-cell foam at rim joists, sloped ceilings and below-grade walls. Mineral wool or fibreglass batts in above-grade exterior walls, with a sealed vapour barrier. Mineral wool in interior walls and floors where sound matters. Blown-in insulation for deep open attic floors. Every house is different, and older Toronto homes especially. We look at the framing, the plans and your budget at the site visit and tell you where foam is worth it and where it is not. Planning a project? We will walk it with you and put it in writing. t: What your drywall sub needs to price a townhouse block accurately
d: Drawings, finish spec, fire separations, ceiling heights and board-ready dates: the information that turns a drywall bid from a guess into a number you can hold.
x: What your drywall sub needs to price a townhouse block accurately Drawings, finish spec, fire separations, ceiling heights and board-ready dates: the information that turns a drywall bid from a guess into a number you can hold. By Ricarti Drywall · 24 November 2026 Open-joist ground floor of a house under construction before insulation and board, Stanton, Toronto. IN SHORT Send architectural drawings with sections, the finish level by area, fire-rated assemblies between units, ceiling heights and bulkheads, the board-ready date and phasing, and site conditions such as access, heat and hoisting. Missing any of these is where change orders come from. Most drywall disputes on new builds start at the bid. A number priced from a floor plan and a guess will be wrong somewhere, and the difference shows up later as an extra. Here is what we ask builders and site supers for, and why. Drawings with sections Floor plans give us wall lengths. Sections and elevations give us ceiling heights, sloped ceilings, stair walls and double-height spaces, which change board size, labour and scaffolding. A full architectural set is best. Finish level by area Level 4 throughout, or Level 5 in great rooms, foyers and stair halls? Garage and mechanical rooms to fire tape only? Name it per area and every bidder is pricing the same job. Fire separations Townhouses and semis need rated separations between units, and garages need separation from the house. The rated assemblies on the drawings, board type, layers and framing, drive material cost and inspection steps. Flag them early. Bulkheads and details Bulkheads for ductwork, coffered ceilings, arches, niches and curved walls take time. If they are not on the drawings yet, tell us where you expect them. Schedule and phasing Board-ready dates for each unit or phase let us staff properly. Ask us what crew size we can commit, and hold us to it. Site conditions Is temporary heat on? Compound needs above-freezing temperatures to cure properly in winter. Can board be hoisted or delivered through openings, or does it go up the stairs? Where can materials be stored, and where does waste go? The more you send, the fewer extras you sign. What you get back A per-unit or per-block price that names the board, insulation and finish levels, the exclusions, and a crew schedule. WSIB clearance and a certificate of insurance come with the quote, not on day one. Send your drawings for pricing. Planning a project? We will walk it with you and put it in writing.
